Lecture 9

Why the integrals commute: the Toda ring is integrable

What this lecture does

Course map: the last step of G1, and the classical half of G5. Lecture 8 found the conserved quantities of the Toda ring — the spectrum of its Lax matrix — and left a debt: conserved is not the same as in involution, and Definition 5.5 asks for both. This lecture pays the debt. It packages all NNN integrals into one function of a spectral parameter, the transfer matrix, proves that its values Poisson-commute from a single identity satisfied by a single site, checks independence, and applies Theorem 5.7: the periodic Toda chain is Liouville integrable, and its motion winds round tori that drift. The identity is the one Lecture 14 quantises.

Reading and tutorial. Material marked Reading is studied on your own; material marked Tutorial is worked in the tutorial. Everything else is the lectured core.

9.1 The question

The Toda ring of Lecture 8 has NNN particles on a circle, H=12∑n=1Npn2+∑n=1Neqn−qn+1,qN+1=q1, H=\frac12\sum_{n=1}^{N}p_n^{2}+\sum_{n=1}^{N}e^{q_n-q_{n+1}}, \qquad q_{N+1}=q_1 , H=21​n=1∑N​pn2​+n=1∑N​eqn​−qn+1​,qN+1​=q1​,(9.1) and its Lax matrix LLL has a spectrum that does not change in time (Theorem 8.2), so the NNN numbers tr⁡Lk\tr L^{k}trLk are conserved. Lecture 8 also rewrote the eigenvalue problem of LLL as a transport from site to site, Φn+1=Ln(λ)Φn\Phi_{n+1}=L_n(\lambda)\Phi_nΦn+1​=Ln​(λ)Φn​, with the 2×22\times22×2 site matrix Ln(λ)=(λ−pne−qn−eqn0),det⁡Ln(λ)=1, L_n(\lambda)=\begin{pmatrix}\lambda-p_n&e^{-q_n}\\ -e^{q_n}&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det L_n(\lambda)=1 , Ln​(λ)=(λ−pn​−eqn​​e−qn​0​),detLn​(λ)=1,(9.2) which contains the variables of site nnn and nothing else.

Definition 5.5 asks for more than conservation: NNN integrals that Poisson-commute with each other and are independent. Nothing in the Lax equation says anything about brackets between the tr⁡Lk\tr L^{k}trLk. So the question of this lecture is

are the Toda ring’s integrals in involution and independent — and if so, what does its motion look like?

The plan has three steps. Build all the integrals at once, as the coefficients of one polynomial t(λ)\transfer(\lambda)t(λ) (§9.2). Show that {t(λ),t(μ)}=0\pb{\transfer(\lambda)}{\transfer(\mu)}=0{t(λ),t(μ)}=0 follows from one identity satisfied by one site matrix (§§9.3 to 9.5). Then independence and Theorem 5.7 do the rest (§§9.6 and 9.7).

9.2 All the integrals at once: the transfer matrix

Transport all the way round the ring.

Definition 9.1 (Monodromy and transfer matrices). For a chain of NNN sites with site matrices Ln(λ)L_n(\lambda)Ln​(λ), the monodromy matrix and the transfer matrix are T(λ)=LN(λ)⋯L2(λ)L1(λ),t(λ)=tr⁡T(λ). \mono(\lambda)=L_N(\lambda)\cdots L_2(\lambda)L_1(\lambda), \qquad \transfer(\lambda)=\tr\mono(\lambda). T(λ)=LN​(λ)⋯L2​(λ)L1​(λ),t(λ)=trT(λ).(9.3) The chain is ultralocal if variables at different sites Poisson-commute: {(Ln)ab,(Lm)cd}=0\pb{(L_n)_{ab}}{(L_m)_{cd}}=0{(Ln​)ab​,(Lm​)cd​}=0 for n≠mn\ne mn=m. When tensor legs are also in play (§9.3), the site moves to a superscript: L(n)=LnL^{(n)}=L_nL(n)=Ln​.

The Toda ring is ultralocal, since LnL_nLn​ involves only (qn,pn)(q_n,p_n)(qn​,pn​). By (9.2), det⁡T=1\det\mono=1detT=1, and T(λ)\mono(\lambda)T(λ) is what a solution of the recursion picks up in one circuit (Figure 9.1).

Hence t(λ)=∑S ∏n∈S(−eqn−qn+1)∏m∉Sˉ(λ−pm), \transfer(\lambda)=\sum_{S}\ \prod_{n\in S}\big(-e^{q_n-q_{n+1}}\big) \prod_{m\notin\bar S}(\lambda-p_m), t(λ)=S∑​ n∈S∏​(−eqn​−qn+1​)m∈/Sˉ∏​(λ−pm​),(9.4) the sum over sets SSS of bonds, no two sharing a site, with Sˉ\bar SSˉ the sites they cover. The same integrals as Lecture 8’s

A number λ\lambdaλ is an eigenvalue of Lecture 8’s Lax matrix LLL exactly when its eigenvalue recursion has a solution with ψn+N=ψn\psi_{n+N}=\psi_nψn+N​=ψn​. The gauge that turned the recursion into Φn+1=Ln(λ)Φn\Phi_{n+1}=L_n(\lambda)\Phi_nΦn+1​=Ln​(λ)Φn​ respects periodicity, since qn+N=qnq_{n+N}=q_nqn+N​=qn​, so this happens exactly when T(λ)\mono(\lambda)T(λ) has an eigenvalue 111: when det⁡(1−T(λ))=2−t(λ)=0\det\big(\Id-\mono(\lambda)\big)=2-\transfer(\lambda)=0det(1−T(λ))=2−t(λ)=0, using det⁡T=1\det\mono=1detT=1. For N≥3N\ge3N≥3, det⁡(λ−L)\det(\lambda-L)det(λ−L) and t(λ)−2\transfer(\lambda)-2t(λ)−2 are both monic of degree NNN. Where the spectrum of LLL is simple they have the same NNN roots, so they are equal there. Such points are dense: at fixed qqq, momenta far enough apart make the discs of Gershgorin’s theorem disjoint and the spectrum simple, so the discriminant of det⁡(λ−L)\det(\lambda-L)det(λ−L) is a non-zero polynomial in ppp, and its non-zero set is dense. Both sides are continuous in (q,p)(q,p)(q,p), so sketched det⁡(λ−L)=t(λ)−2. \det(\lambda-L)=\transfer(\lambda)-2 . det(λ−L)=t(λ)−2.(9.6) The ckc_kck​ are therefore, up to sign and the constant 222, the elementary symmetric functions of the eigenvalues of LLL. Newton’s identities turn them into the tr⁡Lk\tr L^{k}trLk and back. They are Lecture 8’s integrals, reorganised, and they are the candidates for Definition 5.5. Everything now turns on their brackets.

9.3 The notation the proof needs: tensor legs

Ln(λ)L_n(\lambda)Ln​(λ) is a 2×22\times22×2 matrix whose entries are functions on phase space. What we need is the collection of all their brackets, {(Ln)ab(λ),(Ln)cd(μ)}\pb{(L_n)_{ab}(\lambda)}{(L_n)_{cd}(\mu)}{(Ln​)ab​(λ),(Ln​)cd​(μ)}, sixteen functions at once. The trick is to package them as a single 4×44\times44×4 matrix acting on V⊗VV\otimes VV⊗V, with V=C2V=\C^{2}V=C2.

Definition 9.2 (Tensor legs). Write EabE_{ab}Eab​ for the matrix unit with a 111 in row aaa, column bbb, and recall (A⊗B)(ac),(bd)=AabBcd(A\otimes B)_{(ac),(bd)}=A_{ab}B_{cd}(A⊗B)(ac),(bd)​=Aab​Bcd​. For 2×22\times22×2 matrices AAA, BBB put A1=A⊗1\leg{A}{1}=A\otimes\IdA1​=A⊗1, B2=1⊗B\leg{B}{2}=\Id\otimes BB2​=1⊗B, and {A1,B2}=∑a,b,c,d{Aab,Bcd} Eab⊗Ecd,that is({A1,B2})(ac),(bd)={Aab,Bcd}. \pb{\leg{A}{1}}{\leg{B}{2}} =\sum_{a,b,c,d}\pb{A_{ab}}{B_{cd}}\,E_{ab}\otimes E_{cd}, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \Big(\pb{\leg{A}{1}}{\leg{B}{2}}\Big)_{(ac),(bd)}=\pb{A_{ab}}{B_{cd}} . {A1​,B2​}=a,b,c,d∑​{Aab​,Bcd​}Eab​⊗Ecd​,that is({A1​,B2​})(ac),(bd)​={Aab​,Bcd​}.(9.7)

The subscript is a leg, not a matrix index: A1\leg{A}{1}A1​ is the whole matrix AAA, placed in the first factor (Figure 9.2). The right-hand form of (9.7) is the one to memorise: the entry in row (a,c)(a,c)(a,c) and column (b,d)(b,d)(b,d) is the bracket of the (a,b)(a,b)(a,b) entry with the (c,d)(c,d)(c,d) entry.

Remark 9.3 (Two brackets in one formula). A1\leg{A}{1}A1​ and B2\leg{B}{2}B2​ commute as matrices, (A⊗1)(1⊗B)=A⊗B=(1⊗B)(A⊗1)(A\otimes\Id)(\Id\otimes B)=A\otimes B=(\Id\otimes B)(A\otimes\Id)(A⊗1)(1⊗B)=A⊗B=(1⊗B)(A⊗1), because they act in different factors. Their entries do not Poisson-commute: that is what (9.7) records. The composition theorem below turns on the first fact at its decisive step; nothing uses {A1,B2}=0\pb{\leg{A}{1}}{\leg{B}{2}}=0{A1​,B2​}=0, which is false.

One matrix on V⊗VV\otimes VV⊗V appears everywhere below.

Definition 9.4 (Permutation operator). P(v⊗w)=w⊗v\perm(v\otimes w)=w\otimes vP(v⊗w)=w⊗v; equivalently P=∑a,bEab⊗Eba\perm=\sum_{a,b}E_{ab}\otimes E_{ba}P=∑a,b​Eab​⊗Eba​.

Proposition 9.5 (Properties of P\permP). P2=1\perm^{2}=\IdP2=1; P(A⊗B)P=B⊗A\perm(A\otimes B)\perm=B\otimes AP(A⊗B)P=B⊗A, so P\permP commutes with every A⊗AA\otimes AA⊗A; and (Eab⊗Ecd) P  =  Ead⊗Ecb. (E_{ab}\otimes E_{cd})\,\perm \;=\; E_{ad}\otimes E_{cb}. (Eab​⊗Ecd​)P=Ead​⊗Ecb​.(9.8)

Proof. P2\perm^{2}P2 swaps twice. For (9.8), expand P\permP and use EabEef=δbeEafE_{ab}E_{ef}=\delta_{be}E_{af}Eab​Eef​=δbe​Eaf​: the sum ∑e,fδbeEaf⊗δdfEce\sum_{e,f}\delta_{be}E_{af}\otimes\delta_{df}E_{ce}∑e,f​δbe​Eaf​⊗δdf​Ece​ collapses at e=be=be=b, f=df=df=d. 9.4 One identity for one site: the quadratic Sklyanin bracket

Here is the structural assumption that will force involution. It is a statement about the brackets of one site matrix at two values of the spectral parameter, and it involves one fixed numerical matrix.

Definition 9.6 (Quadratic Sklyanin bracket). A site matrix L(λ)L(\lambda)L(λ) satisfies the quadratic Sklyanin bracket with classical r\rmatr-matrix r(λ)\rmat(\lambda)r(λ), a 4×44\times44×4 matrix of numbers, if {L1(λ),L2(μ)}=[r(λ−μ),L1(λ) L2(μ)]for all λ≠μ. \pb{\leg{L}{1}(\lambda)}{\leg{L}{2}(\mu)} =\comm{\rmat(\lambda-\mu)}{\leg{L}{1}(\lambda)\,\leg{L}{2}(\mu)} \qquad\text{for all }\lambda\ne\mu . {L1​(λ),L2​(μ)}=[r(λ−μ),L1​(λ)L2​(μ)]for all λ=μ.(9.9)

The left-hand side is sixteen unknown brackets. The right-hand side says they are all determined by the matrices themselves and one numerical r\rmatr, which is slid past the product L1L2\leg{L}{1}\leg{L}{2}L1​L2​ from both sides (Figure 9.3). Why this form and not another is the content of the next theorem: it is the form that survives multiplication.

Theorem 9.7 (The quadratic bracket composes). If the chain is ultralocal and every site matrix satisfies (9.9) with the same r\rmatr, then so does the monodromy matrix: {T1(λ),T2(μ)}=[r(λ−μ),T1(λ)T2(μ)]\pb{\leg{\mono}{1}(\lambda)}{\leg{\mono}{2}(\mu)} =\comm{\rmat(\lambda-\mu)}{\leg{\mono}{1}(\lambda)\leg{\mono}{2}(\mu)}{T1​(λ),T2​(μ)}=[r(λ−μ),T1​(λ)T2​(μ)].

Proof. Take N=2N=2N=2; the general case is the same telescoping. Leibniz and ultralocality kill the cross terms, and matrices in different legs commute (Remark 9.3), so with A=L1(2)L2(2)A=\leg{L}{1}^{(2)}\leg{L}{2}^{(2)}A=L1(2)​L2(2)​ and B=L1(1)L2(1)B=\leg{L}{1}^{(1)}\leg{L}{2}^{(1)}B=L1(1)​L2(1)​, the two sites’ pairs, {T1,T2}=[r,A]B+A[r,B]=rAB−ArB+ArB−ABr=[r,AB],\pb{\leg{\mono}{1}}{\leg{\mono}{2}} =\comm{\rmat}{A}B+A\comm{\rmat}{B} =\rmat AB-A\rmat B+A\rmat B-AB\rmat =\comm{\rmat}{AB},{T1​,T2​}=[r,A]B+A[r,B]=rAB−ArB+ArB−ABr=[r,AB], and AB=T1T2AB=\leg{\mono}{1}\leg{\mono}{2}AB=T1​T2​, again because leg-111 and leg-222 matrices commute. 

Corollary 9.8 (Commuting transfer matrices). {t(λ),t(μ)}=0\pb{\transfer(\lambda)}{\transfer(\mu)}=0{t(λ),t(μ)}=0 for all λ,μ\lambda,\muλ,μ. Hence the coefficients ckc_kck​ of t(λ)\transfer(\lambda)t(λ) are in involution.

Proof. Take the trace over both factors, tr⁡12(A⊗B)=tr⁡A tr⁡B\tr_{12}(A\otimes B)=\tr A\,\tr Btr12​(A⊗B)=trAtrB: {t(λ),t(μ)}=tr⁡12{T1,T2}=tr⁡12[r,T1T2]=0\pb{\transfer(\lambda)}{\transfer(\mu)} =\tr_{12}\pb{\leg{\mono}{1}}{\leg{\mono}{2}} =\tr_{12}\comm{\rmat}{\leg{\mono}{1}\leg{\mono}{2}}=0{t(λ),t(μ)}=tr12​{T1​,T2​}=tr12​[r,T1​T2​]=0, because the trace of a commutator vanishes. Expanding in λ\lambdaλ and μ\muμ, every coefficient Poisson-commutes with every other. At λ=μ\lambda=\muλ=μ the identity follows by continuity. 

So the whole question of involution has been reduced to one identity for one 2×22\times22×2 matrix. That is where the work of this lecture is.

9.5 The worked example: the Toda site matrix

Proposition 9.9 (The periodic Toda r\rmatr-matrix). On the right of (9.9), write L(λ)=λE11+L0L(\lambda)=\lambda E_{11}+L^{0}L(λ)=λE11​+L0. The permutation commutes with every A⊗AA\otimes AA⊗A (Proposition 9.5), which removes the λμ\lambda\muλμ and the L0⊗L0L^{0}\otimes L^{0}L0⊗L0 terms, and it turns L0⊗E11L^{0}\otimes E_{11}L0⊗E11​ into E11⊗L0E_{11}\otimes L^{0}E11​⊗L0, so [P,L(λ)⊗L(μ)]=(λ−μ)[P,E11⊗L0]=(λ−μ)(L0⊗E11−E11⊗L0)P.\comm{\perm}{L(\lambda)\otimes L(\mu)} =(\lambda-\mu)\comm{\perm}{E_{11}\otimes L^{0}} =(\lambda-\mu)\big(L^{0}\otimes E_{11}-E_{11}\otimes L^{0}\big)\perm .[P,L(λ)⊗L(μ)]=(λ−μ)[P,E11​⊗L0]=(λ−μ)(L0⊗E11​−E11​⊗L0)P. Read the first displayed line as the tensor-leg drill: it is the sixteen brackets of (9.2), of which four are non-zero, written as one 4×44\times44×4 matrix. If that line is not comfortable, nothing after it will be. As an exercise, find the four non-zero brackets and assemble the matrix.

9.6 The theorem

Theorem 9.10 (The periodic Toda chain is Liouville integrable). On R2N\R^{2N}R2N the coefficients c1,…,cNc_1,\dots,c_Nc1​,…,cN​ of t(λ)\transfer(\lambda)t(λ) are in involution and independent on a dense open set, and H=12c12−c2H=\tfrac12c_1^{2}-c_2H=21​c12​−c2​. The periodic Toda chain satisfies Definition 5.5.

Theorem 9.11 (Tori of the ring proved modulo Lemma 5.10 and Theorem 1.9). Let Σ\SigmaΣ be a connected component of a level set of (c1,…,cN)(c_1,\dots,c_N)(c1​,…,cN​) on which dc1,…,dcN\dd c_1,\dots,\dd c_Ndc1​,…,dcN​ are independent at every point, and let Q=1N∑nqnQ=\frac1N\sum_nq_nQ=N1​∑n​qn​ be the centre of mass. Then Σ≅TN−1×R\Sigma\cong T^{N-1}\times\RΣ≅TN−1×R, each slice Σ∩{Q=const}\Sigma\cap\{Q=\text{const}\}Σ∩{Q=const} is a torus TN−1T^{N-1}TN−1, and the flow of HHH is a straight line in the corresponding coordinates.

9.7 The proofs

Proof of Theorem 9.10. Involution is Proposition 9.9, and (9.5) is H=12c12−c2H=\tfrac12c_1^{2}-c_2H=21​c12​−c2​. So {ck,H}=c1{ck,c1}−{ck,c2}=0\pb{c_k}{H}=c_1\pb{c_k}{c_1}-\pb{c_k}{c_2}=0{ck​,H}=c1​{ck​,c1​}−{ck​,c2​}=0: every ckc_kck​ is conserved. Conservation comes out of involution and needs no separate argument.

Independence. Read (9.4): ck=(−1)kek(p)+Rkc_k=(-1)^{k}e_k(p)+R_kck​=(−1)kek​(p)+Rk​, where eke_kek​ is the kkk-th elementary symmetric polynomial of the momenta and every term of RkR_kRk​ has a factor eqn−qn+1e^{q_n-q_{n+1}}eqn​−qn+1​ and degree at most k−2k-2k−2 in ppp (each bond removes two factors λ−p\lambda-pλ−p). In the Jacobian det⁡(∂ck/∂pn)\det(\partial c_k/\partial p_n)det(∂ck​/∂pn​) the part of top degree in ppp therefore comes from the eke_kek​ alone, and it is ±∏i<j(pj−pi)\pm\prod_{i<j}(p_j-p_i)±∏i<j​(pj​−pi​), the Vandermonde determinant. So at fixed qqq the Jacobian is a non-zero polynomial in ppp, which cannot vanish on any open set. Where it does not vanish the dck\dd c_kdck​ are independent; that set is open, and it meets every open set, so it is dense. 

The proof of the second theorem has four steps, and only the first two use the Toda chain at all. Write xn=eqn−qn+1x_n=e^{q_n-q_{n+1}}xn​=eqn​−qn+1​ for the springs.

Proof of Theorem 9.11. (i) Bounded. Every term of HHH is positive. On Σ\SigmaΣ the value H=EH=EH=E is fixed, since HHH is a function of c1c_1c1​ and c2c_2c2​, so ∣pn∣≤2E\abs{p_n}\le\sqrt{2E}∣pn​∣≤2E​ and xn≤Ex_n\le Exn​≤E for every nnn. The springs’ exponents telescope to zero round the ring, so ∏nxn=1\prod_nx_n=1∏n​xn​=1, and each xn=∏m≠nxm−1≥E−(N−1)x_n=\prod_{m\ne n}x_m^{-1}\ge E^{-(N-1)}xn​=∏m=n​xm−1​≥E−(N−1). (By the inequality of arithmetic and geometric means E≥∑nxn≥NE\ge\sum_nx_n\ge NE≥∑n​xn​≥N, so these bounds are not vacuous.) Every gap qn−qn+1q_n-q_{n+1}qn​−qn+1​ therefore lies in [−(N−1)ln⁡E, ln⁡E][-(N-1)\ln E,\,\ln E][−(N−1)lnE,lnE]. Each qn−Qq_n-Qqn​−Q is a fixed linear combination of the gaps, so at fixed QQQ every qnq_nqn​ is bounded too. The slice Σ∩{Q=const}\Sigma\cap\{Q=\text{const}\}Σ∩{Q=const} is closed and bounded: compact.

(ii) Complete. Let G=∑ktkckG=\sum_kt_kc_kG=∑k​tk​ck​ for constants tkt_ktk​. By involution HHH is constant along the flow of GGG, so the bounds of (i) hold along every integral curve. The components of XG\hvf{G}XG​ are polynomials in the pnp_npn​ and the xnx_nxn​, hence bounded by a constant CCC on the curve, which in a time τ\tauτ moves at most a distance CτC\tauCτ and so stays in a compact ball. By the escape argument of Proposition 1.7, a curve that exists only up to a finite time must leave every compact set. So every such flow is complete.

(iii) Cylinder. Stages (i)–(iii) of the proof of Theorem 5.7 and the first half of stage (iv) (§5.5) use involution, independence on Σ\SigmaΣ, connectedness and complete flows, and nothing else. They make Σ\SigmaΣ the orbit of an action of RN\R^{N}RN with a discrete stabiliser Λ\LambdaΛ, so Σ≅RN/Λ\Sigma\cong\R^{N}/\LambdaΣ≅RN/Λ (Lemma 5.10).

(iv) Drift. Shifting every pnp_npn​ by sss is the same as shifting λ\lambdaλ by −s-s−s in (9.4), so ∑n∂ck/∂pn\sum_n\partial c_k/\partial p_n∑n​∂ck​/∂pn​ is a constant multiple of ck−1c_{k-1}ck−1​, constant on Σ\SigmaΣ. Hence QQQ changes at a constant rate along each flow, and QQQ at the time-sss point is Q(x0)+ℓ(s)Q(x_0)+\ell(s)Q(x0​)+ℓ(s) for a linear map ℓ:RN→R\ell:\R^{N}\to\Rℓ:RN→R, not zero since ℓ(e1)=−1\ell(e_1)=-1ℓ(e1​)=−1. A period does not move QQQ, so Λ⊂ker⁡ℓ≅RN−1\Lambda\subset\ker\ell\cong \R^{N-1}Λ⊂kerℓ≅RN−1, and Σ∩{Q=Q(x0)}≅ker⁡ℓ/Λ\Sigma\cap\{Q=Q(x_0)\}\cong\ker\ell/\LambdaΣ∩{Q=Q(x0​)}≅kerℓ/Λ. Step (i) is the only place the ring matters. On the open chain nothing ties the springs together, a single spring can be made as weak as one likes at fixed energy, and the level sets stay unbounded even after the drift is removed: the open chain scatters instead of winding.

9.8 What it buys

The motion. On every regular level set the flow of HHH is a straight line in coordinates on TN−1×RT^{N-1}\times\RTN−1×R: it winds round the torus while the centre of mass moves along R\RR at the constant speed ∑npn/N\sum_np_n/N∑n​pn​/N, possibly zero. For N=3N=3N=3, with the centre of mass removed, the tori meet the Poincaré section of Figure 7.5 in its closed curves: the numerical plot of Lecture 7, beside the chaos of Hénon–Heiles at the same energy, illustrates this theorem at E=1/6E=1/6E=1/6.

Action–angle variables need one more step. Separate the centre of mass canonically, fix the total momentum, and N−1N-1N−1 relative degrees of freedom remain, whose regular level sets are the compact tori of Theorem 9.11. To those Theorem 6.5 applies. As an exercise, carry out the separation for N=2N=2N=2 with Q=(q1+q2)/2Q=(q_1+q_2)/2Q=(q1​+q2​)/2, 2pˉ=p1+p22\bar p=p_1+p_22pˉ​=p1​+p2​, x=q1−q2x=q_1-q_2x=q1​−q2​ and px=(p1−p2)/2p_x=(p_1-p_2)/2px​=(p1​−p2​)/2; the two-particle ring at the end of the readings does it. Computing the actions needs the curve z+1/z=t(λ)z+1/z=\transfer(\lambda)z+1/z=t(λ) of the reading below, with one action for each of its N−1N-1N−1 gaps cited: Flaschka and McLaughlin 1976.

The method. Three moves did everything, and none of them is special to Toda:

  1. one identity, (9.9), for one site matrix;

  2. composition along the chain, Theorem 9.7, which needs only ultralocality;

  3. the trace, which kills a commutator.

Change the site matrix and the r\rmatr-matrix, and the same three moves give commuting integrals for another chain. Lecture 14 replaces the Poisson bracket by the commutator and r\rmatr by an R\RmatR-matrix with R=1+iℏ r+O(ℏ2)\Rmat=\Id+\ii\hbar\,\rmat+O(\hbar^{2})R=1+iℏr+O(ℏ2). The same three moves then give the commuting transfer matrices of the Heisenberg spin chain, and on the quantum Toda chain their limit ℏ→0\hbar\to0ℏ→0 is exactly (9.9) with (9.10). That is goal G5, and the one row of the classical-to-quantum dictionary that is a theorem rather than an analogy.

9.9 Caveats, in one place

Three things a careful reader should know, collected here so that the arguments above can run without interruption. (The linear bracket, which this lecture does not need, is in the reading.)

  1. Independence is generic, not universal. Theorem 9.10 proves independence on a dense open set, and that is all Definition 5.5 asks. It does fail somewhere: at the equilibrium pn=0p_n=0pn​=0, xn=1x_n=1xn​=1 every flow is a drift.

  2. The ring drifts. The flow of c1=−∑npnc_1=-\sum_np_nc1​=−∑n​pn​ translates every qnq_nqn​ and changes no spring, so no level set is compact. Tori appear only after the centre of mass is fixed, which is why Theorem 9.11 is stated for slices.

  3. The sign of r\rmatr belongs to the site matrix. Other books use the site matrix with e±qe^{\pm q}e±q exchanged, which gives r=+P/λ\rmat=+\perm/\lambdar=+P/λ; mixing a sign with the wrong site matrix breaks (9.9).

9.10 The same integrals from zero curvature, and the route not taken

Conservation directly. (Lecture 8’s reading has the fuller version, with the plaquette picture.) Involution gave conservation for free, but t(λ)\transfer(\lambda)t(λ) is also conserved for a more geometric reason. With Vn(λ)=(−λ/2−e−qneqn−1λ/2)V_n(\lambda)=\big(\begin{smallmatrix}-\lambda/2&-e^{-q_n}\\ e^{q_{n-1}}&\lambda/2\end{smallmatrix}\big)Vn​(λ)=(−λ/2eqn−1​​−e−qn​λ/2​), the equations of motion of the ring are equivalent to L˙n=Vn+1Ln−LnVn\dot L_n=V_{n+1}L_n-L_nV_nL˙n​=Vn+1​Ln​−Ln​Vn​ for every nnn and every λ\lambdaλ: transport in space and in time commute round every plaquette of the space-time lattice, a discrete zero-curvature condition. The route not taken. One can prove integrability of the open chain instead: its N×NN\times NN×N Lax matrix satisfies the linear bracket with a constant r\rmatr, the involution theorem for that bracket gives {tr⁡Lj,tr⁡Lk}=0\pb{\tr L^{j}}{\tr L^{k}}=0{trLj,trLk}=0, and independence follows from a band lemma for tridiagonal matrices. Its bracket does not compose, so it cannot be quantised site by site, and it is the ring’s quadratic bracket that Lecture 14 quantises.

The spectral curve. Setting det⁡(z−T(λ))=0\det\big(z-\mono(\lambda)\big)=0det(z−T(λ))=0 gives z+1/z=t(λ)z+1/z=\transfer(\lambda)z+1/z=t(λ), since det⁡T=1\det\mono=1detT=1. 9.11 The route not taken, I: the linear bracket

The core proved the ring’s integrals commute through the quadratic bracket, because it composes. The older route goes through a bracket linear in LLL, for a single Lax matrix; the open-chain reading below applies it.

Definition 9.12 (Sklyanin bracket). A Lax matrix L(λ)L(\lambda)L(λ) satisfies a Sklyanin bracket with classical r\rmatr-matrix r\rmatr if {L1(λ),L2(μ)}  =  [r12(λ−μ),L1(λ)+L2(μ)], \pb{\leg{L}{1}(\lambda)}{\leg{L}{2}(\mu)} \;=\;\comm{\leg{\rmat}{12}(\lambda-\mu)}{\leg{L}{1}(\lambda)+\leg{L}{2}(\mu)}, {L1​(λ),L2​(μ)}=[r12​(λ−μ),L1​(λ)+L2​(μ)],(9.11) where r12(λ)\leg{\rmat}{12}(\lambda)r12​(λ) is a matrix on V⊗VV\otimes VV⊗V of numbers — it does not depend on the point of phase space.

Read what (9.11) asserts. On the left is an arbitrary d2×d2d^{2}\times d^{2}d2×d2 matrix of Poisson brackets, d4d^{4}d4 functions on phase space with no reason to be related. On the right is a commutator of one fixed numerical matrix with something built linearly from LLL itself. The assumption is enormously restrictive, and its whole force is that the same r\rmatr works at every point of phase space and for every pair λ,μ\lambda,\muλ,μ.

Two qualifications:

  • Numerical. If r\rmatr is allowed to depend on the dynamical variables the bracket is called dynamical, and optional lecture B meets the first real example — Calogero–Moser has no r\rmatr of the constant form. Everything proved in the involution theorem below survives that generalisation; the classical Yang–Baxter equation of Lecture 14’s reading does not.

  • Which r\rmatr? Part I teaches how to read and check an r\rmatr-matrix, never how to solve for one. Finding r\rmatr from scratch is outside it.

Remark 9.13 (r\rmatr is not arbitrary). Antisymmetry of the Poisson bracket already constrains r\rmatr. Reading (9.7) backwards, {Lab,Lcd}=−{Lcd,Lab}\pb{L_{ab}}{L_{cd}}=-\pb{L_{cd}}{L_{ab}}{Lab​,Lcd​}=−{Lcd​,Lab​} is the matrix statement {L1(λ),L2(μ)}=−P {L1(μ),L2(λ)} P\pb{\leg{L}{1}(\lambda)}{\leg{L}{2}(\mu)}=-\perm\,\pb{\leg{L}{1}(\mu)}{\leg{L}{2}(\lambda)}\,\perm{L1​(λ),L2​(μ)}=−P{L1​(μ),L2​(λ)}P. Substituting (9.11) on both sides and writing r21=P r12 P\leg{\rmat}{21}=\perm\,\leg{\rmat}{12}\,\permr21​=Pr12​P, the two agree as soon as r12(λ)=−r21(−λ). \leg{\rmat}{12}(\lambda)=-\leg{\rmat}{21}(-\lambda). r12​(λ)=−r21​(−λ).(9.12) The rational r(λ)=cP/λ\rmat(\lambda)=c\perm/\lambdar(λ)=cP/λ satisfies it, since P P P=P\perm\,\perm\,\perm=\permPPP=P makes r21=r12\leg{\rmat}{21}=\leg{\rmat}{12}r21​=r12​ there, and cP/λc\perm/\lambdacP/λ is odd. The classical Yang–Baxter equation of Lecture 14’s reading uses (9.12) to trade r21\leg{\rmat}{21}r21​ for −r12-\leg{\rmat}{12}−r12​.

This pays Lecture 8’s debt by the route not taken. Note how little was spent: the argument never opened r\rmatr, never used the Lax equation, and never mentioned a Hamiltonian. It also never used the particular combination L1+L2\leg{L}{1}+\leg{L}{2}L1​+L2​ — only that it commutes with AAA.

Corollary 9.15 (What the model gets). Expanding tr⁡L(λ)k\tr L(\lambda)^{k}trL(λ)k in powers of λ\lambdaλ produces a family of functions in involution, and any Hamiltonian among them has all the others as commuting integrals. Whether there are nnn independent ones is a separate question about the model, settled for the open Toda chain in the open-chain reading below.

The converse: Babelon–Viallet

Theorem 9.14 is one-way: a Sklyanin bracket gives involution. The converse is true but weaker than one would like.

Theorem 9.16 (Babelon–Viallet cited). If the eigenvalues of LLL are in involution on a neighbourhood where LLL is regular and semisimple, then LLL satisfies {L1,L2}=[r12,L1]−[r21,L2], \pb{\leg{L}{1}}{\leg{L}{2}} =\comm{\leg{\rmat}{12}}{\leg{L}{1}}-\comm{\leg{\rmat}{21}}{\leg{L}{2}}, {L1​,L2​}=[r12​,L1​]−[r21​,L2​],(9.15) with r\rmatr in general dynamical — a function on phase space.

Read (9.15) carefully: it is not (9.11). Two independent matrices appear, and the single-commutator form is the special case r21=−r12\leg{\rmat}{21}=-\leg{\rmat}{12}r21​=−r12​. The converse does not deliver that special case, and the difference is not a technicality — it is the difference between a true statement and a false one.

Example 9.17 (Why the strengthening fails). On a canonical (q,p)(q,p)(q,p) plane put D=diag⁡(a,b)D=\operatorname{diag}(a,b)D=diag(a,b) with a≠ba\ne ba=b, and L(q,p)=UDU−1,U=eqE12epE21.L(q,p)=U D U^{-1},\qquad U=e^{qE_{12}}e^{pE_{21}} .L(q,p)=UDU−1,U=eqE12​epE21​. Then LLL is regular semisimple near the origin and its eigenvalues are the constants a,ba,ba,b, so they are in involution for the most trivial of reasons. At the origin ∂qL=[E12,D]=(b−a)E12\partial_qL=\comm{E_{12}}{D}=(b-a)E_{12}∂q​L=[E12​,D]=(b−a)E12​ and ∂pL=[E21,D]=(a−b)E21\partial_pL=\comm{E_{21}}{D}=(a-b)E_{21}∂p​L=[E21​,D]=(a−b)E21​, so {L12,L21}∣0=−(a−b)2≠0.\pb{L_{12}}{L_{21}}\Big|_{0}=-(a-b)^{2}\ne0 .{L12​,L21​}​0​=−(a−b)2=0. Now look at where that number would have to come from in (9.11). At the origin L1+L2=D⊗1+1⊗D\leg{L}{1}+\leg{L}{2}=D\otimes\Id+\Id\otimes DL1​+L2​=D⊗1+1⊗D is diagonal with entries 2a, a+b, a+b, 2b2a,\,a+b,\,a+b,\,2b2a,a+b,a+b,2b, and the required entry sits between the two equal ones. For any matrix r\rmatr whatever, dynamical or not, a commutator with a diagonal matrix has that entry multiplied by the difference of the two diagonal entries — here zero. So no r\rmatr can satisfy (9.11) for this LLL, while (9.15), with its two independent terms, has no such obstruction.

So an r\rmatr-matrix always exists behind involution, but it need not be numerical and it need not put the bracket in the single-commutator form of Definition 9.12. The classification of solutions of the classical Yang–Baxter equation (Lecture 14’s reading) applies to neither. Optional lecture B meets a dynamical r\rmatr in Calogero–Moser, so the caveat is not hypothetical.

Three particles, by hand.

For N=3N=3N=3 the traces are F1=∑pnF_1=\sum p_nF1​=∑pn​, F2=∑pn2+2(a12+a22)F_2=\sum p_n^{2}+2(a_1^{2}+a_2^{2})F2​=∑pn2​+2(a12​+a22​) and F3=∑pn3+3a12(p1+p2)+3a22(p2+p3)F_3=\sum p_n^{3}+3a_1^{2}(p_1+p_2)+3a_2^{2}(p_2+p_3)F3​=∑pn3​+3a12​(p1​+p2​)+3a22​(p2​+p3​). The torus conclusion of Theorem 5.7 is not claimed for the open chain, and it is false. Lecture 12’s reading shows that k=0k=0k=0: every fibre is a copy of RN\R^{N}RN, with no periodic direction at all. If this feels like a let-down after so many tori, it is the point. The definition of integrability is algebraic (Definition 5.5); the torus is a theorem, with a hypothesis, and here the hypothesis fails. What the open chain does on its non-compact fibres is the subject of Lecture 12: it scatters.

Both are real symmetric, so every band edge is real; spectral duality, below, shows that there are 2N2N2N of them, counted with multiplicity.

Figure 9.6 shows t(λ)\transfer(\lambda)t(λ) for a six-particle ring: N=6N=6N=6 bands, where it crosses the strip ∣t∣≤2\abs{\transfer}\le2∣t∣≤2 monotonically, and N−1=5N-1=5N−1=5 gaps, where it turns round outside it (Corollary 9.30 proves this is general). The momenta keep changing; the band edges do not.

At the equilibrium, all qnq_nqn​ equal and all pn=bp_n=bpn​=b, every an=1a_n=1an​=1 and one finds t(λ)=2TN((λ−b)/2)\transfer(\lambda)=2T_N\big((\lambda-b)/2\big)t(λ)=2TN​((λ−b)/2), with TNT_NTN​ the Chebyshev polynomial: it touches ±2\pm2±2 at every turning point, all gaps are closed, and the spectrum is the single band [b−2,b+2][b-2,b+2][b−2,b+2] of the free tight-binding model. Example 9.28 (All gaps closed: the equilibrium). At q1=⋯=qNq_1=\dots=q_Nq1​=⋯=qN​ and p1=⋯=pN=bp_1=\dots=p_N=bp1​=⋯=pN​=b every an=1a_n=1an​=1, and L(z)L(z)L(z) is the free tight-binding model. Outside codimension-two loci every gap is open (Henrici–Kappeler, cited), but a special excitation need not open them all (for N=4N=4N=4, a state repeating with period 222 has t=d2−2\transfer=d^{2}-2t=d2−2, ddd the two-site trace, and two of its three gaps stay closed). The curve as a two-sheeted cover.

Above each λ\lambdaλ lie two points of Γ\GammaΓ, z+z_+z+​ and z−=1/z+z_-=1/z_+z−​=1/z+​, which coincide exactly at the band edges. So Γ\GammaΓ is two copies of the λ\lambdaλ-plane (the sheets) glued along cuts joining the band edges in pairs; crossing a cut exchanges zzz and 1/z1/z1/z (Figure 9.7). With all gaps open, 2N2N2N branch points and NNN cuts give a closed surface with N−1N-1N−1 handles: genus N−1N-1N−1 (Babelon–Bernard–Talon, §6.2 cited), the dimension of the tori of Theorem 9.11. The actions below say why.

A warning on names. Babelon–Bernard–Talon exchange the letters: their λ\lambdaλ is our zzz, their μ\muμ our λ\lambdaλ, their 2t(μ)2t(\mu)2t(μ) our t(λ)\transfer(\lambda)t(λ), and their n+1n+1n+1 particles our NNN (so their genus nnn is our N−1N-1N−1).

Spectral duality: one curve, read two ways

Proposition 9.26 matched the two eigenvalue problems as sets. The polynomial identity is sharper.

Theorem 9.29 (Spectral duality). For N≥3N\ge3N≥3 and all λ∈C\lambda\in\Cλ∈C, z≠0z\ne0z=0,   det⁡(λ−L(z))=t(λ)−(z+1z)   \boxed{\;\det\big(\lambda-L(z)\big)=\transfer(\lambda)-\Big(z+\frac1z\Big)\;} det(λ−L(z))=t(λ)−(z+z1​)​(9.27) The left side is the characteristic polynomial of the N×NN\times NN×N Lax matrix, whose spectral parameter is zzz; the right side is the characteristic equation of the 2×22\times22×2 monodromy matrix, whose spectral parameter is λ\lambdaλ. They define the same curve Γ\GammaΓ.

The matrix λ−L(z)\lambda-L(z)λ−L(z) is tridiagonal apart from its corners, −aNz-a_Nz−aN​z at (N,1)(N,1)(N,1) and −aN/z-a_N/z−aN​/z at (1,N)(1,N)(1,N). Likewise the other corner alone gives −1/z-1/z−1/z, and every other term uses both corners or neither and does not involve zzz. Then det⁡(λ−L(z))=0\det(\lambda-L(z))=0det(λ−L(z))=0, so λ\lambdaλ is an eigenvalue of L(z)L(z)L(z), so by Proposition 9.26 z+1/z=t(λ)z+1/z=\transfer(\lambda)z+1/z=t(λ). The merged N=2N=2N=2 matrix satisfies (9.27) too (scripts/check-l10-algebra.py, N=2,…,5N=2,\dots,5N=2,…,5, symbolic).

Two spectral parameters, one curve.

  • zzz, the Bloch–Floquet multiplier, lives in the corners of the N×NN\times NN×N matrix L(z)L(z)L(z). Fix zzz: NNN points of Γ\GammaΓ, the eigenvalues of L(z)L(z)L(z). Γ\GammaΓ is an NNN-sheeted cover of the zzz-plane.

  • λ\lambdaλ, the energy of the Bloch wave, is the spectral parameter of the 2×22\times22×2 site matrices. Fix λ\lambdaλ: 222 points of Γ\GammaΓ, the eigenvalues z,1/zz,1/zz,1/z of T(λ)\mono(\lambda)T(λ). Γ\GammaΓ is a two-sheeted cover of the λ\lambdaλ-plane.

  • The eigenvalue of one Lax matrix is the spectral parameter of the other. The Flaschka normalisation was chosen so that this holds with no factor.

Figure 9.8 draws the NNN-sheeted reading over the unit circle ∣z∣=1\abs{z}=1∣z∣=1: the familiar band diagram of a crystal. A vertical line meets it in NNN points, a horizontal line inside a band in 222.

Duality pays off at once.

What zzz does and does not buy

An honest remark: zzz gives no new integrals. Expanding (9.27) with Newton’s identities, tr⁡L(z)k=tr⁡Lk(k<N),tr⁡L(z)N=tr⁡LN+N(z+1z−2).\tr L(z)^{k}=\tr L^{k}\quad(k<N),\qquad \tr L(z)^{N}=\tr L^{N}+N\Big(z+\frac1z-2\Big).trL(z)k=trLk(k<N),trL(z)N=trLN+N(z+z1​−2). The zzz-dependence is carried by a1⋯aNa_1\cdots a_Na1​⋯aN​, a constant by (8.11): L(z)L(z)L(z) holds exactly the integrals LLL had. Contrast Manakov’s parameter in §8.11, which recovered a missed integral.

Where the spectral parameter is indispensable. In the 2×22\times22×2 formulation: all NNN integrals are the coefficients of one 2×22\times22×2 trace, and without λ\lambdaλ the site matrices carry nothing. In the bracket: (9.9) compares λ\lambdaλ with μ\muμ, and without it there is no composition along the ring; Lecture 14 quantises exactly this, with T(λ)\mono(\lambda)T(λ) operator-valued, RTTRTTRTT in place of (9.9), and t(λ)\transfer(\lambda)t(λ) generating a spin-chain Hamiltonian. And in the geometry: the actions of the tori of Theorem 9.11 are periods of the curve.

Action variables from the curve.

When all N−1N-1N−1 gaps are open, the curve has N−1N-1N−1 closed loops that stay over the real axis (a closed gap collapses its loop to a point): above the jjj-th gap, both roots z±z_\pmz±​ are real, and the loop runs along the gap on one sheet and back on the other, crossing between them at the two band edges (Figure 9.9). Call it αj\alpha_jαj​.

The same region, sliced two ways.

This is the sense in which the genus of Γ\GammaΓ equals the dimension of the tori: each open gap is a handle of the curve and a circle of the torus, and its width measures how hard that circle is excited. Theta functions on Γ\GammaΓ then give the motion itself in closed form (Babelon–Bernard–Talon, §6.4 cited), which we do not pursue.

Summary

  • All integrals at once. The monodromy T=LN⋯L1\mono=L_N\cdots L_1T=LN​⋯L1​ and the transfer matrix t=tr⁡T\transfer=\tr\monot=trT (Definition 9.1); its coefficients c1,…,cNc_1,\dots,c_Nc1​,…,cN​ include H=12c12−c2H=\tfrac12c_1^{2}-c_2H=21​c12​−c2​ (9.5), and they are Lecture 8’s integrals reorganised, det⁡(λ−L)=t(λ)−2\det(\lambda-L)=\transfer(\lambda)-2det(λ−L)=t(λ)−2 (9.6).
  • Tensor legs. {A1,B2}\pb{\leg{A}{1}}{\leg{B}{2}}{A1​,B2​} has (ac),(bd)(ac),(bd)(ac),(bd) entry {Aab,Bcd}\pb{A_{ab}}{B_{cd}}{Aab​,Bcd​}; different legs commute as matrices (Remark 9.3).
  • One identity for one site. The quadratic Sklyanin bracket (9.9) composes along an ultralocal chain (Theorem 9.7), and its trace gives {t(λ),t(μ)}=0\pb{\transfer(\lambda)}{\transfer(\mu)}=0{t(λ),t(μ)}=0 (Corollary 9.8).
  • Toda. The site matrix satisfies it with r=−P/λ\rmat=-\perm/\lambdar=−P/λ (Proposition 9.9); with the Vandermonde argument, the ring is Liouville integrable (Theorem 9.10), and its regular level sets are TN−1×RT^{N-1}\times\RTN−1×R (Theorem 9.11). Goal G1 is reached.
  • Next. Part II begins: Lecture 10 constructs the Heisenberg chain’s eigenstates by Bethe’s guess, Lecture 14 quantises this lecture’s three moves into commuting transfer matrices, and Lecture 15 diagonalises them and recovers the Bethe equations.
